paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 2000, the average weekday edition of a British national newspaper sold around two million copies. Today, the figure is closer to half a million for the best-selling title, and several regional papers have closed altogether. The cause appears obvious: people now read the news online, often for free. But the story is more complicated than a simple move from paper to screen.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One complication is that readership has not fallen as sharply as sales. Many newspapers now reach more people than ever through their websites. The Guardian, for instance, has more than a hundred million monthly visitors worldwide. The difficulty is that online readers bring far less money. A print reader pays a cover price and also attracts advertisers willing to pay high rates. An online reader may read three articles, see a few cheap advertisements and leave.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Several newspapers have responded by asking readers to pay. The New York Times has more than nine million subscribers, a model many publishers admire. But the success is not universal. Large national titles with international appeal can persuade people to pay, while small local papers struggle, because their readers can find similar information on social media for nothing. The result is so-called news deserts: areas where no one regularly reports on the local council, courts or schools.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The consequences matter for democracy. Studies from the United States found that in towns where the local newspaper closed, fewer people stood for election, and local government spending rose, possibly because fewer journalists were checking how money was used. These findings do not prove that closure caused the changes, but they are troubling.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some countries are testing solutions. Canada requires large technology companies to pay publishers when their articles appear on their platforms, while in Norway the government gives financial support to local news. Critics fear that state money could threaten independence. Others argue that news is a public good, like roads or lighthouses, and that society has a duty to pay for it. The debate is likely to continue as the old model fades.
